claims.text: Previously reported HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations and domain morphologies.
A multi-fidelity model with explicit chemical-fluctuation and domain-morphology descriptors will accurately predict Young’s modulus in hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework will accurately predict yield strength in hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework will accurately predict fracture toughness in hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
Combining a reduced number of high-level calculations with surrogate models can reduce reliance on costly atomistic calculations.
First-principles searches over multi-principal-element alloy design spaces are impeded by high computational demands.
Microstructural variables such as domain size, local composition fluctuations, and phase distribution contain information relevant to mechanical-property prediction.
Explicit hierarchical-microstructure descriptors allow the model to represent subtle strengthening mechanisms.
Encoding chemical-fluctuation length scales and morphology allows the model to capture heterogeneous deformation.
Encoding chemical-fluctuation length scales and morphology allows the model to capture crack-bridging phenomena.
The proposed descriptors can represent the relevant deformation and fracture behavior without exhaustive ab initio or continuum simulation of every candidate.
The proposed model will improve relative predictive accuracy by approximately 20–30% over prior single-fidelity or purely ab initio approaches.
The proposed model will reduce high-performance-computing demand by approximately 70%.
Previous composition-only single-fidelity models have lower predictive accuracy than the proposed hierarchical model.
The model becomes unreliable when domain size, phase fraction, or local elemental-distribution descriptors fall outside its training domain.
The model becomes unreliable when processing or temperature produces phases or nanoprecipitates absent from the training data.
The numerical accuracy and computing-efficiency gains are based on prior HPC–ML demonstrations.
Calibrated ASTM test protocols provide consistent measurements of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness.
